subject: physics
title: Mass, volume and density
summary: Tell mass from weight, measure the volume of liquids and irregular solids, and use density to predict whether an object floats or sinks.
objectives: Measure volume with a measuring cylinder and by the displacement method
Calculate density using density = mass ÷ volume
Use density to predict whether an object floats or sinks

sections.title: Why does a log float but a copper nail sink?
sections.body:
A big log can float down the Kafue River, yet a tiny copper nail from the Copperbelt sinks straight to the bottom. The log is far heavier, so weight alone cannot explain this.

The answer is density: how much mass is packed into each cubic centimetre of a material. In this lesson you will learn to measure mass and volume, and then use them to find density.

sections.title: Mass and weight are not the same
sections.body:
Mass is the amount of matter in an object. Its SI unit is the kilogram (kg). We measure mass with a beam balance or an electronic balance. Your mass is the same in Lusaka, on top of a mountain, or on the Moon.

Weight is the pull of gravity on an object. Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons (N) with a spring balance. On Earth, gravity pulls with about 10 N on every 1 kg. On the Moon, gravity is about one-sixth as strong, so your weight there is about one-sixth of your weight on Earth, but your mass does not change.
bullets: Mass: amount of matter, in kg, measured with a balance, the same everywhere
Weight: pull of gravity, in N, measured with a spring balance, changes from place to place

sections.question: An astronaut with a mass of 70 kg travels to the Moon. What happens to her mass and weight?
options: Her mass stays the same, but her weight becomes smaller
Her mass and weight both stay the same
sections.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter, and she has not lost any matter, so her mass stays 70 kg. Weight is the pull of gravity, and the Moon pulls about one-sixth as hard, so her weight falls. It is the weight, not the mass, that becomes about one-sixth.

sections.title: Measuring volume
sections.body:
Volume is the amount of space something takes up. The SI unit is the cubic metre (m³), but in the laboratory we usually use cm³. 1 cm³ is the same as 1 millilitre (ml), and 1 litre = 1000 cm³.

For a regular solid, like a box shape (a cuboid), calculate: volume = length × width × height.

For a liquid, use a measuring cylinder on a flat bench. The surface of water curves down slightly in the middle. This curve is called the meniscus. Read the bottom of the meniscus, with your eye level with it, to avoid parallax error. (Mercury is different: its meniscus curves up, so you read the top.)

sections.title: Worked example: volume of a regular block
sections.problem: A wooden block is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 2 cm high. Find its volume.
steps: Step 1: The block is a cuboid, so volume = length × width × height.
Step 3: 5 × 4 = 20, and 20 × 2 = 40. The unit is cm × cm × cm = cm³.
sections.answer: The volume of the block is 40 cm³.

sections.title: Irregular solids: the displacement method
sections.body:
A stone has no neat length, width or height, so we cannot use a formula. Instead we use the displacement method. When the stone goes under water, it pushes aside (displaces) its own volume of water, so the water level rises.

Pour some water into a measuring cylinder and read the level. Tie the stone to a thread and lower it gently until it is fully under water. Read the new level. The volume of the stone is the difference between the two readings.

Volume of solid = final reading − first reading.

sections.question: A measuring cylinder contains 40 cm³ of water. A key is lowered in and the level rises to 55 cm³. What is the volume of the key?
sections.explanation: Volume of the key = final reading − first reading = 55 − 40 = 15 cm³. 55 cm³ is the volume of the water and key together, not the key alone. 95 cm³ adds the readings instead of subtracting.

sections.title: Density = mass ÷ volume
sections.body:
Density tells us how much mass there is in each unit of volume. Its symbol is ρ, the Greek letter rho.

Density = mass ÷ volume, or ρ = m ÷ V.

If mass is in g and volume is in cm³, density is in g/cm³. The SI unit is kg/m³. To change g/cm³ to kg/m³, multiply by 1000. Water has a density of 1.0 g/cm³, which is 1000 kg/m³. Some other values: ice 0.92 g/cm³, aluminium 2.7 g/cm³, copper 8.96 g/cm³, mercury 13.6 g/cm³.

The triangle helps you rearrange the formula. Cover the quantity you want and read what is left.

sections.title: Worked example: density of a stone
sections.problem: The stone in the displacement diagram has a volume of 18 cm³. Its mass, measured on a balance, is 45 g. Find its density in g/cm³ and in kg/m³.
steps: Step 1: Write the formula: density = mass ÷ volume.
Step 2: Put in the values with units: density = 45 g ÷ 18 cm³.
Step 4: To change to kg/m³, multiply by 1000: 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 kg/m³.
sections.answer: The density of the stone is 2.5 g/cm³ (2500 kg/m³).

sections.title: Worked example: finding mass from density
sections.problem: Cooking oil has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³. What is the mass of 500 cm³ of cooking oil?
steps: Step 1: Cover m in the triangle: mass = density × volume.
Step 3: 0.92 × 500 = 460. The cm³ units cancel, leaving g.
sections.answer: The mass of the oil is 460 g.

sections.title: Common mistake: mixing units in the density formula
sections.body:
A learner writes the mass of the stone as 0.045 kg and its volume as 18 cm³, then works out 0.045 ÷ 18 = 0.0025. This answer has the strange unit kg/cm³ and is easy to misread.

Before you divide, make the units match. Either use g with cm³ (45 g ÷ 18 cm³ = 2.5 g/cm³) or kg with m³. Also remember that heavy does not mean dense. A large log is heavy, but its density is less than that of water.

sections.title: Floating and sinking
sections.body:
Whether an object floats or sinks in a liquid depends on comparing densities, not on size or weight.

The wooden block from earlier has a volume of 40 cm³. If its mass is 24 g, its density is 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6 g/cm³. This is less than water (1.0 g/cm³), so it floats.
bullets: Object less dense than the liquid: it floats. Ice (0.92 g/cm³) floats on water.
Object denser than the liquid: it sinks. Copper (8.96 g/cm³) sinks in water.
Liquids follow the same rule: cooking oil floats on top of water.
Even iron (about 7.9 g/cm³) floats on mercury (13.6 g/cm³).

sections.question: A block has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 40 cm³. What happens when it is placed in water?
options: It sinks, because its mass is more than 1 g
It floats, because its density is 0.75 g/cm³, which is less than water
It sinks, because its density is 1.33 g/cm³
It floats, because its volume is a bigger number than its mass
sections.explanation: Density = 30 g ÷ 40 cm³ = 0.75 g/cm³. This is less than 1.0 g/cm³, so the block floats. 1.33 g/cm³ comes from dividing volume by mass, the wrong way round. Comparing the bare numbers for volume and mass is not a reliable rule; you must work out the density.

sections.title: Key points
bullets: Mass is the amount of matter (kg, balance) and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity (N, spring balance) and changes.
1 cm³ = 1 ml and 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Read the bottom of a water meniscus with your eye level with it.
Volume of an irregular solid = final water level − first water level (displacement method).
Density = mass ÷ volume. Units: g/cm³ or kg/m³ (multiply g/cm³ by 1000 to get kg/m³).
An object floats if it is less dense than the liquid and sinks if it is denser.

quiz.question: What is the SI unit of mass?
quiz.explanation: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg). The newton is the unit of weight, which is a force. The litre and cubic centimetre are units of volume.

quiz.question: Which instrument measures weight?
quiz.explanation: Weight is a force, and a spring balance measures force in newtons. A beam balance compares masses, a measuring cylinder measures volume, and a vernier caliper measures small lengths.

quiz.question: Which of these is equal to 1 cm³?
quiz.explanation: 1 cm³ is exactly the same volume as 1 millilitre. A litre is much bigger: 1 litre = 1000 ml = 1000 cm³.

quiz.question: The water in a measuring cylinder is at 35 cm³. When a stone is lowered in, the level rises to 47 cm³. What is the volume of the stone?
quiz.explanation: Volume of stone = final reading − first reading = 47 − 35 = 12 cm³. 47 cm³ is the water and stone together, and 82 cm³ adds the readings instead of subtracting.

quiz.question: A metal cube has a mass of 120 g and a volume of 15 cm³. What is its density?
quiz.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume = 120 g ÷ 15 cm³ = 8 g/cm³. 1800 comes from multiplying, and 0.125 comes from dividing volume by mass, the wrong way round.

quiz.question: Fresh milk has a density of about 1.03 g/cm³. What is the mass of 2 litres of milk?
quiz.explanation: First change litres to cm³: 2 litres = 2000 cm³. Then mass = density × volume = 1.03 × 2000 = 2060 g. 1942 g comes from dividing by the density instead of multiplying, and 2000 g ignores the density.

quiz.question: Why does ice float on water?
options: Ice is always lighter than any amount of water
The density of ice (0.92 g/cm³) is less than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³)
quiz.explanation: Floating depends on density. Ice is less dense than water, so it floats. A large iceberg is much heavier than a cup of water, so "lighter" is not the reason, and ice certainly has mass.

quiz.question: A copper block is cut into two equal halves. What is the density of each half?
options: It depends on the shape of each half
The same as the original density
quiz.explanation: Each half has half the mass and half the volume. Density = mass ÷ volume, so (m ÷ 2) ÷ (V ÷ 2) = m ÷ V, which is unchanged. Density is a property of the material, not of the size of the piece.

glossary.definition: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg). It is the same everywhere.
The pull of gravity on an object. It is a force, measured in newtons (N).
The amount of space an object takes up, measured in m³ or cm³.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube, such as a measuring cylinder.
Finding the volume of an irregular solid by measuring how much the water level rises when it is put under water.
Mass per unit volume of a material: density = mass ÷ volume, in g/cm³ or kg/m³.
